title: The “anti-social century” with Derek Thompson
gist: A podcast intro framing Derek Thompson's “anti-social century” thesis — a 21st-century rise in time spent alone — with Yglesias worried that home-entertainment tech is isolating people and driving sadness that liberals need to explain, while co-host Jerusalem distinguishes benign aloneness from harmful loneliness.

insights.claim: Derek Thompson coined “the anti-social century” to describe a large 21st-century rise in the amount of time people spend alone.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A named, spreading cultural frame for social atomization is a demand-side signal for solo-consumption categories (home entertainment, delivery, gaming) and a headwind for out-of-home social venues.
insights.quote: Derek Thompson coined the phrase “the anti-social century” to describe an incredible rise over the course of the 21st century in the amount of time that people spend alone.

insights.claim: Recent technological progress has concentrated in home-entertainment pursuits that leave people spending more time alone and lacking human connection.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Ties the isolation trend directly to where tech investment has flowed, implying continued tailwinds for at-home digital media and pressure on the social/experiential economy.
insights.quote: Recent technological progress has been very concentrated in the realm of home entertainment pursuits that have left people spending more time alone and lacking human connection.
insights.locator: This is an issue I’m concerned about

insights.claim: Co-host Jerusalem argues for distinguishing loneliness from aloneness, saying evidence for a rise in aloneness is much clearer than for a rise in loneliness and that being alone is fine as long as it is not making people lonely and sad.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Whether solo living reads as benign or harmful shapes whether policy and product markets treat it as a problem to solve or a preference to serve.
insights.quote: There’s nothing wrong, she argues, with people being alone as long as it’s not making them lonely and sad.

insights.claim: Yglesias contends that people increasingly are sad and angry even if they do not report being lonely.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Reframes social malaise as under-reported, suggesting sentiment surveys may understate the affective downside of atomization.
insights.quote: people increasingly are sad and angry even if they don’t say that they are lonely

insights.claim: People who espouse moderate or liberal politics need an explanation for bad social vibes that does not cede the substantive ground to illiberal forces.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Frames social isolation as contested political terrain, implying the malaise narrative is a live electoral asset for illiberal movements if the center-left ignores it.
insights.quote: people who espouse moderate or liberal politics need some explanation for bad vibes that doesn’t cede the substantive ground to illiberal forces
